findings.source_quote: Ἐπεὶ πυκνότερόν σε ὁρῶ τὸν λόγον ποιούμενον ὑπὲρ τοῦ πλάσαντός σε θεοῦ
findings.english_quote: Since I see you speaking so persistently on behalf of the God who fashioned you
findings.issue: The draft substitutes persistence for the frequency expressed by πυκνότερόν and does not represent its comparative form. Even an elative interpretation would concern speaking quite frequently, rather than necessarily speaking persistently.
findings.suggested_revision: Use “Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you.” If an elative rendering such as “quite frequently” is preferred, document that interpretation.

findings.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἂν ὁ τὰ πάντα γινώσκων θεὸς (ὡς ἐκ πολλῶν ἔστιν δεῖξαι) ἐπείραζεν, ἵνα γνῷ αὐτός, ὁ τὰ πάντα προγινώσκων.
findings.english_quote: For God, who knows everything, would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand, as can be shown from many passages.
findings.issue: The parenthetical qualification follows God's knowing everything in the Greek. Moving it to the sentence's end changes the clause order and makes it read as support specifically for the final foreknowledge statement.
findings.suggested_revision: Restore the parenthesis's placement: “For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand.”

findings.source_quote: οὔτε ἀπὸ ·γραφῶν οὔτε ὑφ’ ἑτέρου τινὸς σκανδαλισθῆναι δυνάμεθα οὔτε πολλοὺς θεοὺς ἀποδέξασθαι ἀπατώμεθα
findings.english_quote: we can neither be made to stumble by scriptures or anyone else, nor be deceived into accepting many gods
findings.issue: The English extends “can” over both coordinated predicates. In the Greek, δυνάμεθα governs being made to stumble, whereas ἀπατώμεθα independently states that they are not deceived into accepting many gods. The draft strengthens that second assertion into an inability to be deceived.
findings.suggested_revision: Distinguish the predicates: “Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.”

findings.source_quote: λέγω δὲ ὡς ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν γεννώμενον Ἐμμανουὴλ καὶ τὸν λεγόμενον θεὸν ἰσχυρόν.
findings.english_quote: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and the one who wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God.
findings.issue: The first two participles share a single article, ὁ, naturally presenting one subject who spoke and wrestled. The draft repeats “the one,” presenting them as independently enumerated figures and obscuring the contrast with the subsequently repeated τὸν. Although the English does not necessarily assert distinct identities, the material shared-subject reading is not clearly represented or discussed in the notes.
findings.suggested_revision: Use “I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God.” Explain that the first two participles share one article and that this motivates the shared-subject rendering. If retaining a distributive interpretation instead, document its grammatical basis and preserve the shared-subject alternative without asserting necessarily distinct identities.
